title: Bidirectional Dijkstra in Sapporo: FASTER Routes!
description: Watch Bidirectional Dijkstra visualize how two synchronized shortest-path searches meet in the middle to reach a target efficiently. On Sapporo’s street grid-style graph, you’ll see explored nodes shrink dramatically versus one-way search.
ig_caption:
🗺️❄️ Sapporo streets, but make it math—welcome to **Bidirectional Dijkstra**! In this visualization, we run two Dijkstra frontiers: one expanding from the start node and another from the goal node. ✅ They advance by the lowest tentative distance (priority queue), and the moment their visited/relaxed regions overlap, we can reconstruct the shortest path with far fewer explored intersections than classic one-direction search.

📌 **Deep technical idea:** each side maintains distances (g-values) over the same weighted graph, and when a connecting node is found, the best candidate path is updated using the combined costs. Because Dijkstra is guaranteed optimal on non-negative edge weights, this “meet-in-the-middle” strategy preserves correctness while accelerating convergence on large road graphs.

🧠 **Graph theory on real maps:** treat the city street network as a weighted graph—nodes are intersections, edges are road segments (distance/time). Bidirectional Dijkstra reduces the search space, especially when the shortest path is not near the start or goal.

yt_description:
Bidirectional Dijkstra Visualization in Sapporo (Chuo-ku)! 🗺️❄️

In this YouTube Shorts video, we demonstrate **Bidirectional Dijkstra**, a shortest-path algorithm that launches two Dijkstra searches—one from the start and one from the target—and stops when the frontiers meet to efficiently find the optimal route.

🎯 Keywords: Bidirectional Dijkstra, shortest path, pathfinding visualization, Dijkstra algorithm, graph search, priority queue, weighted graph, road network, real-world map.

⏱️ Mechanics: Two priority queues expand by lowest tentative distance; when overlap occurs, we combine costs to reconstruct the best path.
